## 1. Your question and data

1. State your question in one sentence. If it changed since your exploratory analysis, briefly explain how and why.

Did kelp forests in Southern California long-term marine protected areas (MPAs) have better resistance to the 2014-2016 marine heatwave (MHW) than unprotected Southern California Kelp Forests? Resistance defined as less change in the observed statistic (biomass/fish count or type count/pct canopy) from before (2011-2013) to during (2014-2016) and during to after (2017-2019).

This is slightly more focused than my EDA question, but similar. I narrowed the scope to Southern California instead of California and Oregon, and want to narrow down to only "long-term" MPAs vs their associated reference. I've also identified more exact response variables - fish biomass, count, or type count, also possibly percent canopy (38% missing data in that column of my dataset). The year ranges for before, during, and after are also set now based on background research for the specific Southern California MHW timeline.

2. In one paragraph, give the context for your question: why it matters, to whom, and what is already known about it. Cite at least **two sources** (these can be scientific literature, news articles, government reports, or any other reputable source).

As climate change continues to contribute to global ocean warming, kelp forest environments remain under threat. These communities are vital to maintain, both for economic (fishing and tourism industries) and environmental (marine carbon sequestration, biodiversity, coastal protection) purposes. Generally the larger kelp species that form the backbone of these unique aquatic communities - such as Giant Kelp and Bull Kelp - require cooler water temps to survive, and the negative effects of kelp forest ecosystem decline with ocean warming have been well studied (Kelp Forest Alliance 2024, Ober 2025). However, there is ongoing research continuing to study whether California's history of MPA usage has helped protected kelp forests be more resilient to the effects of marine warming. Some of these studies have found that MPAs have helped kelp species recover more quickly from heatwave events (Ober 2025), while others have found the MPAs had no effect on the "ecological resistance" of these kelp forests (Smith 2023).

Jansen, C. (2023, February 1). Utilising kelp forests for carbon sequestration. Earth.Org. [https://earth.org/kelp-forests-carbon-sequestration/](https://earth.org/kelp-forests-carbon-sequestration/)

Kelp Forest Alliance. (2024). 2.0 Kelp ecosystem services. In State of the world's kelp report. [https://kelpforestalliance.com/state-of-the-worlds-kelp-report/2-0-kelp-ecosystem-services/](https://kelpforestalliance.com/state-of-the-worlds-kelp-report/2-0-kelp-ecosystem-services/)

Ober, H. (2025, August 26). Marine protected areas keep California's kelp resilient against rising water temperatures, scientists find. UCLA Newsroom. [https://newsroom.ucla.edu/releases/marine-protected-areas-protect-help-climate-change](https://newsroom.ucla.edu/releases/marine-protected-areas-protect-help-climate-change)

Smith, J. G., et al. (2023). A marine protected area network does not confer community structure resilience to a marine heatwave across coastal ecosystems. Global Change Biology, 29, 5634–5651. [https://doi.org/10.1111/gcb.16862](https://doi.org/10.1111/gcb.16862)

3. Describe your data in a few sentences: the source, who collected it and how, what one row represents, and the response variable you're most interested in.

This dataset has been assembled by several UCSC and UCSB scientists, and their teams of SCUBA diver observers, as part of the PISCO kelp forest monitoring program. This program collects observational data for fish, kelp, and invertebrates (ecological and some physical attributes) from kelp forests in California and southern Oregon to track community dynamics through various events that occur over time (i.e. MHWs). One row in the main dataset I'm planning to use - the PISCO kelp forest fish data - records observed metrics for a single taxa (classcode) observed in a single transect at a specific site on a specific date. For the purposes of this proposal assignment, I'm using types of taxa observed as my response variable, but as noted earlier I'm still considering biomass or some version of a organism count.

Citation: Mark H. Carr, Jennifer E. Caselle, Daniel P. Malone, Avrey Parsons-Field, & Katelin D. Seeto. (2026). PISCO Kelp Forest Community Surveys. PISCO MN. [doi:10.6085/AA/PISCO_kelpforest.1.11](https://doi.org/10.6085/AA/PISCO_kelpforest.1.11).

4. Include the one figure from your exploratory analysis (or create a new one) that best shows the relationship between your response and explanatory variables.

```{r}
# Load packages
library(tidyverse)
library(here)
library(ggpubr)
```

```{r}
# Load data
# Fish transect-level survey
fish_df <- read_csv(here('final_project','data','PISCO_kelpforest_fish.1.11.csv'))
# Site table (MPA status)
site_df <- read_csv(here('final_project','data','PISCO_kelpforest_site_table.1.11.csv'))
# Taxa table (Classcode definition)
taxa_df <- read_csv(here('final_project','data','PISCO_kelpforest_taxon_table.1.11.csv'))
```

```{r}
# Find columns to merge on btwn fish and site dfs
shared_cols_fish <- intersect(colnames(fish_df), colnames(site_df))
print(shared_cols_fish)

# Filter sites df before join
site_filt_df <- site_df |> 
                filter((campus == "UCSB") & ((site_status == "mpa") | (site_status == "reference"))) |> 
                group_by(site) |>  
                slice(1) |> 
                ungroup() |> 
                select(site, MPA_Name, mpa_type, site_status)

# Merge mpa status to fish df
fish_mpa_df <- fish_df |> 
                # Filter to relevant years
                filter((survey_year >= 2011) & (survey_year <= 2019) & (campus == "UCSB")) |> 
                # Remove unecessary and duplicate columns
                select(-campus,-year,-method) |> 
                # Calculate species richness (number of taxa per transect per obs. date)
                summarise(species_richness = n(),
                          .by = c(survey_year,month,day,site,zone,level,transect)) |> 
                # Join to site_filt_df
                inner_join(site_filt_df,
                           by = join_by(site)
                           ) |> 
                # Create MHW year categories
                mutate(MHW_Category = ifelse(
                            (survey_year >= 2014 & survey_year <= 2016),
                            "During",
                            ifelse(
                                (survey_year >= 2017),
                                "After",
                                "Before"
                            )
                ))
```

```{r}
# Plot bar plot for "Before" MHW
plt1 <- fish_mpa_df |> 
    mutate(`MPA Status` = site_status) |>
    filter(MHW_Category == "Before") |> 
    ggplot(aes(x = survey_year,
                y = species_richness,
                fill = `MPA Status`)) +
    geom_bar(stat = "identity", position = "dodge") +
    theme_bw() +
    labs(title = "Before MHW (2011-2013)",
         x = "Survey Year",
         y = "Species Richness (Taxa Count)")

# Plot bar plot for "During" MHW
plt2 <- fish_mpa_df |> 
    mutate(`MPA Status` = site_status) |>
    filter(MHW_Category == "During") |> 
    ggplot(aes(x = survey_year,
                y = species_richness,
                fill = `MPA Status`)) +
    geom_bar(stat = "identity", position = "dodge") +
    theme_bw() +
    labs(title = "During MHW (2014-2016)",
         x = "Survey Year",
         y = "Species Richness (Taxa Count)")

# Plot bar plot for "After" MHW
plt3 <- fish_mpa_df |> 
    mutate(`MPA Status` = site_status) |>
    filter(MHW_Category == "After") |> 
    ggplot(aes(x = survey_year,
                y = species_richness,
                fill = `MPA Status`)) +
    geom_bar(stat = "identity", position = "dodge") +
    theme_bw() +
    labs(title = "After MHW (2017-2019)",
         x = "Survey Year",
         y = "Species Richness (Taxa Count)")

# Arrange plts in one figure
figure = ggarrange(plt1,plt2,plt3, nrow = 1, ncol = 3, common.legend = TRUE, legend = "bottom")
annotate_figure(figure, top = "MPA Status and Taxa Species Richness")
```
**Figure 1:** Bar plots showing fish taxa species richness (number of taxa per transect observation) in MPA and reference areas before, during, and after the 2014-2016 MHW.

## 2. Causal relationships

1. Draw a directed acyclic graph (DAG) of the causal relationships you think connect your explanatory variable to your response. Include at least one other variable that affects your response, and at least one potential **confounder** (a variable that affects both your explanatory and response variables). You may draw it by hand and include a photo, or use a tool like `mermaid` (see below).
2. Explain each arrow in your DAG in one sentence. Why do you think that causal relationship exists?
3. Which variables in your DAG are in your data? Which are not? How might the missing variables bias your results?

> [!TIP]
> Recall the Simpson's paradox example from this homework: the relationship between distance to the freeway and soil lead changed substantially once we accounted for area. A DAG is how you anticipate problems like that _before_ fitting your model.

> [!TIP]
> [Mermaid](https://quarto.org/docs/authoring/diagrams.html) is a tool for making diagrams that you can use in Quarto to make DAGs. Here's an example of a DAG where $x_1$ and $x_2$ have causal effects on $y$, and $x_2$ has an effect on $x_1$. In this example, $x_2$ is a _confounder_ of the relationship between $x_1$ and $y$.

```{mermaid}
flowchart LR
  %% Water temp affects nutrient and prey availability for predator species
  water_temp --> species_richness
  %% PH affects nutrient and prey availability for predator species
  pH --> species_richness
  %% MPA_status affects fishing/harvesting/outside access which impacts species richness
  MPA_status --> species_richness
  %% Pollution can make water more or less acidic depending on the pollution type
  pollution --> pH
  %% Pollution can introduce poisons to the ecosystem
  pollution --> species_richness
  %% Climate change effects can reduce the number of species
  climate change --> species_richness
  %% Climate change effects can increase water temp
  climate change --> water_temp
```

Pollution and pH are not in my dataset, which could introduce bias into my results as both have potentially major effects on species survivability in kelp forests. Water temp (w/ 38% missing data) and climate change/MHW (through years and dates) are in my dataset.

Scientific Hypothesis: Kelp forests in long-term MPAs in Southern California had better resilience to the 2014-2016 MHW event than unprotected Southern California kelp forests.

Statistical H_null: MPA status had no effect on species richness before, during, or after the 2014-2017 MHW in Southern California.

Statistical H_alt: Kelp forests in Southern California MPAs had less change in species richness before, during, and after the 2014-2016 MHW compared to unprotected Southern California kelp forests.
